subject: anatomy
title: Lymphoid Organs, Histology and Microvascular Architecture

steps.tx: Lymph nodes are encapsulated bean-shaped secondary lymphoid organs arranged along lymphatic vessels. Histologically, a lymph node is divided into an outer cortex, an intermediate paracortex, and an inner medulla. The outer **lymph node cortex** contains spherical lymphoid follicles packed with B lymphocytes, dedicated to humoral immune activation.
steps.say: Lymph nodes are encapsulated lymphoid organs filtering tissue lymph. Histologically, each node features an outer cortex, paracortex, and inner medulla. The outer cortex houses spherical lymphoid follicles packed with B cells that mediate humoral immunity.

vis.alt: Lymph node architecture: cortex, follicles, paracortex, and medulla
vis.caption: Lymph node histology showing cortical B-cell and paracortical T-cell zones. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Primary lymphoid follicles are uniform aggregates of resting, mature B cells. Upon antigenic stimulation, a follicle activates into a secondary follicle displaying a pale **germinal centre** surrounded by a dark mantle zone. The germinal centre is the anatomical site where B cells undergo clonal proliferation, somatic hypermutation, and antibody affinity maturation.
steps.say: Primary follicles consist of resting B cells. Following antigen stimulation, they convert into secondary follicles displaying a pale germinal centre wrapped by a dark mantle zone. Germinal centres drive B-cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation, and affinity maturation.

left.title: Primary Follicle
points: Packed with naive resting B lymphocytes

right.title: Secondary Follicle
points: Dark mantle zone of naive B cells

steps.tx: Deep to the superficial cortex lies the **paracortex**, representing the T-cell dependent zone of the lymph node. It contains specialized post-capillary venules designated high endothelial venules, lined by plump cuboidal endothelial cells. High endothelial venules express selectins and addressins that guide circulating naive T and B lymphocytes out of blood into lymph parenchyma.
steps.say: Beneath the cortex lies the paracortex, the T-cell dependent zone of the lymph node. It houses high endothelial venules lined by cuboidal endothelial cells expressing adhesion molecules that capture circulating lymphocytes into the node.

steps.tx: The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ, lacking lymphatic vessel inflow and filtering circulating blood directly. It comprises white pulp and red pulp separated by a marginal zone. The **white pulp** is organized around central arterioles: periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) contain T lymphocytes, while adjacent splenic follicles contain B lymphocytes.
steps.say: The spleen filters blood directly without lymphatic afferents. Comprising white and red pulp, its white pulp arranges around central arterioles: periarteriolar sheaths contain T cells, while adjacent follicles contain B lymphocytes.

vis.alt: Splenic histology: white pulp, central arteriole, and red pulp sinusoids
vis.caption: Splenic microarchitecture: white pulp PALS and red pulp filtration cords. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The splenic **red pulp** consists of blood-filled venous sinusoids separated by cellular splenic cords of Billroth. Cords are packed with macrophages, plasma cells, and reticular fibres. Aging red blood cells with rigid membranes cannot squeeze through the narrow endothelial slits of sinusoids and are phagocytosed by cordal macrophages, mediating extravascular hemolysis.
steps.say: Splenic red pulp contains blood sinusoids separated by cellular cords of Billroth packed with macrophages. Aging red cells with stiffened membranes cannot squeeze through endothelial slits into sinusoids and are engulfed by cordal macrophages.

points: PALS houses CD4+ and CD8+ T cells
Follicles generate IgM and IgG antibodies
Primary site for opsonization of bacteria

right.title: Red Pulp Functions
points: Cords of Billroth and venous sinusoids

steps.tx: The primary lymphoid organ for T-cell education is the **thymus**, situated in the anterior superior mediastinum. The thymus features an outer cortex where immature thymocytes undergo positive selection, and an inner medulla containing whorled concentric keratinised epithelial structures called Hassall corpuscles (thymic corpuscles), which instruct regulatory T-cell development.
steps.say: The primary lymphoid organ for T-cell education is the thymus in the anterior mediastinum. It contains an outer cortex where thymocytes undergo positive selection and an inner medulla marked by concentric epithelial Hassall corpuscles that foster regulatory T cells.

rows: Immature double-positive T cells, nurse cells
Blood-thymus barrier protects from blood antigens
Overlying microfold M cells in gut

steps.tx: Blood vessel walls are organized into three concentric tunics. The innermost **tunica intima** comprises a single layer of endothelium resting upon a subendothelial connective tissue bed and the internal elastic lamina. The middle tunica media contains circularly arranged smooth muscle cells and elastic lamellae, while the outer tunica adventitia contains collagen and vasa vasorum.
steps.say: Blood vessels feature three concentric tunics. The innermost tunica intima consists of endothelium and internal elastic lamina. The middle tunica media contains smooth muscle and elastic laminae, while the outer adventitia houses collagen and nutrient vasa vasorum.

rows: One to two layers of smooth muscle
Primary site of systemic vascular resistance

steps.tx: Capillaries are classified into three architectural varieties: continuous capillaries possess an uninterrupted endothelial lining with tight junctions, found in the brain and muscle. **Fenestrated capillaries** exhibit transcellular pores bridged by delicate diaphragms, facilitating rapid filtration in renal glomeruli, intestinal villi, and endocrine glands. Discontinuous sinusoidal capillaries feature wide gaps in liver and spleen.
steps.say: Capillaries are categorized into continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal varieties. Continuous capillaries line brain and muscle with tight junctions. Fenestrated capillaries bear microscopic pores for filtration in kidneys and gut, while sinusoidal capillaries allow cell passage in liver and spleen.
